source_title: 'You are helping by carrying your shopping' poster
source_collection: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
source_description:
This poster was printed in Britain during the Second World War (1939-45) to remind people to conserve fuel resources which were rationed. 
 
 It was donated to Te Papa by Wellington businessman Mr Cecil H. Andrews. He collected many such posters during the war and distributed them to his clients for display in their shop windows, such as McKenzies, James Smith’s and Woolworths. This particular poster would have been just as resonant in New Zealand as in Britain, as petrol was rationed here from 1939-46. 
 
 The poster shows an ordinary person going about their business, which is often a feature of Second World War posters. Civilians were frequently targeted by government campaigns – to volunteer for service, to give money, to recycle and conserve resources. In the Second World War everyone was expected to play a part, and it would have been hard to escape the direct appeal of colourful posters like this on city streets.

It was assumed that the Japanese would continue their southward advance and invade and conquer Australia. source_title: Poster, 'there's a MAN'S job to be done'
source_collection: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
source_description: \n This poster was one of the first voluntary recruitment posters to be commissioned by the Army Department at the beginning of the Second World War. It was critical for the government to stimulate enthusiasm for voluntary enlistment, partly in the hope of avoiding conscription. The strongly gendered image and message in this poster appealed to masculine ideals of work, honour and commitment. Here war equals work, and a regular soldier does the calling, not the government. \n Very few examples of this poster have survived, and very few are held in public institutions. With the introduction of compulsory military service in June 1940, recruitment posters 'were of course abandoned, and except for a few copies retained for historical purposes no special effort was made to preserve them' (Director of Publicity to C. H. Bateson, 24 April 1941, External Affairs, series 1, 84/12/12, part 1, Archives New Zealand).

source_description: The New Zealand government financed the Second World War (1930-45) from internal resources, raising substantial amounts through taxation, internal loans and savings. Posters such as this one played a significant part in the associated fund-raising campaigns, making intense appeals to New Zealanders' sense of patriotism and sacrifice. This particular poster was part of a National Savings movement begun by the New Zealand Government in October 1940 to develop a 'thrift' habit among citizens. The Minister of Finance entrusted the administration of the National Savings Act 1940 to a special committee - the New Zealand National Savings Committee. The National Savings Committee delegated the development of the campaign to the Post Office, but the general scheme and the national publicity arrangements remained with the Committee (including the publishing of posters such as this example).

source_description:
This Second World War poster was one of 150,000 posters, window stickers, grille cards and strips produced in 31 different designs and sizes for the Victory Loan campaign of August 1944. The Victory Loan aimed to raise £40 million over a five-week period (28 August to 4 October) to help meet the costs of New Zealand's war expenditure, which was at its highest in the year of 1943-44. 
 This poster was considered 'campaign ammunition' and would have been seen in shop and business windows, railway stations, hotel lobbies, post offices, sport gatherings and campaign meetings. The large scale of the Victory Loan required a 'Campaign Handbook' which detailed the importance of posters and how to use them. 
 The image in this poster is particularly romantic with its heroic-looking airman gazing up at the machinery of war in the sky.

source_description: This poster advertises a march for a Hiroshima Day in the 1980s. At the end of the Second World War, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. Both cities were devastated. At least 70,000 people were killed instantly in the Hiroshima blast and 40,000 instantly in the Nagasaki blast, with tens of thousands more dying or suffering from radiation in years to come. These atomic bombs were the first to be used in war and they kick-started the nuclear-arms race.

 Greenpeace 
 Greenpeace was founded in 1971 in response to nuclear weapons testing by the United States. In 1972, Greenpeace held its first protest against French testing at Moruroa.

source_description: This poster by David Blair visualises the catastrophic risks to peace posed by the nuclear-armed Trident missile. In his image, a dove of peace is fatally pierced as a missile launches towards the sky. The Trident is a submarine-launched ballistic missile. The first Trident was launched by the United States Navy in 1977, and adopted by Britain in the 1990s. Both programmes were met with sustained protests by the anti-nuclear movement. Blair was part of Auckland Artists Action which began as Artists Against Apartheid during the Springbok rugby tour in 1981. The 'AAA' logo bottom right of the poster, was designed by Stanley Palmer during the tour.

source_title: Poster, 'The World According to Ronald Reagan'
source_collection: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
source_description:
This poster presents an ironic map of the world according to United States President Ronald Reagan (1981-89). Nothing is geographically correct, but possibly how many believed it to be in the 1980s. The world is divided between Republicans ('and other real Americans'); those who are useful politically or economically (eg 'Our Oil'); and everyone else (eg 'Democrats and Welfare Bums'). 
 Many nations do not count in this world view. New Zealand is simply attached to Australia with both being dismissed as 'Kangaroos'. 
 During Ronald Reagan's first term, the Cold War was the most pressing foreign policy issue. He embarked on a massive build-up of weapons and troops. In 1983, he announced the Strategic Defense Initiative, a plan aiming to develop space-based weapons to protect America from attacks by Soviet nuclear missiles.

source_title: 'International Women's Day for Nuclear Disarmament' poster
source_collection: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
source_description:
This poster was produced for a demonstration in Wellington on 24 May 1983 when a large group of women roped themselves around the perimeter of the Department of Defence headquarters building in Stout Street, Wellington. Their protest was peaceful and was part of the International Women’s Day for Nuclear Disarmament (which had originated in Europe). 
 Impact of protest 
 According to a Defence staff member who was in the building at the time, this was an emotional moment. The men in the office were 'full of bravado' but when the women linked hands, they fell silent.

source_collection: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
source_description: \n This poster protested against the visit of the USS Texas to Wellington on 10 August 1983. Over 10,000 people marched in a lunch-time protest during the ship's visit, including School Children Against the Texas (SCAT). Posters and slogans were plastered up throughout the city. \n The poster was created by the Coalition Against Nuclear Warships (CANWAR, founded in 1976) which was a coalition of peace groups opposed to nuclear-armed or powered ships visiting New Zealand ports. For example, Wellington received five such visits between 1976 and 1984: USS Truxton in August 1976, September 1980 and May 1982; the USS Texas in August 1983; and the HMS Invincible in August 1984. As in other ports, each visit was met with protests in the city and on the harbour, with the Peace Squadron confronting the vessels.

source_description:
This poster was designed by cartoonist and illustrator Trace Hodgson for Greenpeace a month after the French bombing and sinking of its protest ship Rainbow Warrior in July 1985. 
 The Rainbow Warrior was moored in Auckland when two bombs ripped through it. The ship’s photographer died retrieving his camera. The crew had been preparing to set sail for Moruroa to protest against French nuclear weapon testing. 
 The poster was screenprinted by Chris McBride and Dave Kent of Wellington Media Collective in an edition of 500. Dave Kent's expertise with technique, colour and composition enhanced the original illustration.

source_collection: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
source_description:
This poster advertises a concert by the Herbs held at Victoria University in 1985. 
 The Herbs are a popular New Zealand group producing 'homegrown' music that has become synonymous with New Zealand's cultural identity. They are also among New Zealand's first reggae music bands to produce original, conscious reggae exploring important local issues such as New Zealand's anti-nuclear stance, the Rainbow Warrior affair, and Maori land rights (such as the occupation of Bastion Point). 
 The poster design is infused with the Rastafarian colours of black, red, green and gold (yellow in the case of this poster).

Both cities were devastated. At least 70,000 people were killed in the Hiroshima blast, with many thousands more dying or suffering from radiation in years to come. These atomic bombs were the first to be used in war and they kick-started the nuclear-arms race.

source_description:
This poster by the Wellington branch of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament protests against French power and nuclear testing in the Pacific. 
 Between 1966 and 1996, France carried out about 190 nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls in French Polynesia. These caused reef damage, landslides, subsidence, radioactive emissions, and fish poisoning. 
 The poster features the logo for the Nuclear Free and Independent Pacific Movement. The movement was formed in 1980 to widen the struggle against nuclear testing in the Pacific to independence from colonial powers.

source_description: \n This poster advertises a march to take place in Wellington, New Zealand, on 4 August 1990, calling for independence from United States military influence in New Zealand. The poster states: \n 'ANZUS: In or out of it, we must exclude the nuclear warships of all nations from our ports. ANZUS links New Zealand to the United States military strategy, through tracking and communications facilities such as Black Birch and Tangimoana, and through the US base at Harewood. Through the 'Memorandum of Understanding', New Zealand has agreed to act as a US base in times of tension. This can only increase the risk of New Zealand becoming a target in the event of nuclear war.'

source_collection: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
source_description:
This poster calls for people to join a demonstration against the visit of French Prime Minister Michel Rocard to Wellington, New Zealand on 29 April 1991. 
 The protest was against French nuclear testing in the Pacific. Between 1966 and 1996, France carried out about 190 nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls in French Polynesia. These caused reef damage, landslides, subsidence, radioactive emissions, and fish poisoning. 
 Community spirit 
 The poster is interesting for its sense of humour and community spirit - not only was there to be a deadly serious demonstration - live entertainment was provided for the crowds turning up to demonstrate.

source_description: Artwork by Arrernte artist Helen Kemarre Shearer. Of the artwork Shearer writes: 'These are my Dreaming stories from my mother's and my father's country - Arrernte Dreaming tracks. I lived at Atitjere Homelands, which is Harts Range on the white fellas map. Dreaming’s represented are the snake, yalka (bush onion), tjaipa (witchetty grub), honey ant and the seven sisters. Alangwa is shown as a vital food supply which is constant and a strength to and for the people. The hands symbolise the passing down of our Dreaming stories for our future generations.'
source_notes: Maintain the Dreaming-Our Culture is Our Heritage

source_description: \n This poster commemorates Hiroshima Day, 6 August 1992, in New Zealand. \n The poster features an image of ground zero in Hiroshima. At the end of the Second World War, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. Both cities were devastated. At least 70,000 people were killed in the Hiroshima blast, with many thousands more dying or suffering from radiation in years to come. These atomic bombs were the first to be used in war and they kick-started the nuclear-arms race.
